In this experiment you will recognize the RADAR indicator blocks on the PC130-231 experiment card. U3 represents the Synchro Amplifier, Timer, Range Mark Generator, and Video Amplifier. U3 also provides a target generator for simulation purposes.
IUUIIGGIIU
In an actual RADAR system a target generator would not be used except, perhaps, in testing the RADAR system. U2 represents the Sweep Generator.

The PC130-231 card will allow you to simulate a simple A Scan display. This type of display is commonly used in military applications, particularly in weapons control systems. It has the ability of providing the target range as well as the relative strength of a returned echo.
The most important aspect of any RADAR system is timing. The purpose of the timing section is to synchronize the entire RADAR system. No RADAR can operate properly unless system timing is accurate...
The modulator, transmitter, antenna and display must be triggered to ensure that the system is operable.
IUUIIGGIIU

Master timing for the circuit is provided by the main timer U3A and associated circuitry. These components form an oscillator. A Schmitt trigger converts a sawtooth waveform into a squarewave. The output from the main timer provides the timing for the other sections that comprise the RADAR simulator...

C2 and R2 determine the length of time for the output of the main timer, while U3B inverts the signal to a squarewave pulse. The function of this section is to produce a squarewave output with a fixed width for use as a timing pulse. All other functions in the RADAR simulator are triggered by the leading edge of this pulse...

The sweep amplifier (U2) produces a sawtooth waveform that is used to drive the electron beam across the face of the RADAR indicator. The sawtooth wave is based on the charge/discharge time of capacitors C3 and C4...

The sawtooth is started by the inverted timing pulse. The low pulse discharges the capacitors. After the pulse, the capacitors are allowed to charge. The charging action of the capacitors are amplified by U2...
R9, the ramp adj potentiometer controls the charge rate of the capacitors. The charge rate determines the slope of the sweep.

A Range Mark Generator and Amplifier produce repetitive marks that appear at fixed distances on the sweep of the indicator. Range marks provide the operator with an indication of distance to the target under surveillance...
Range marks appear as intensified lines on the face of the CRT. The number of range marks appearing on the Indicator is dependent upon the length or range of the sweep.
The sweep on a RADAR indicator can represent distances anywhere from 1 mile to 300 miles. As an example, if the sweep represented 20 miles, the range marks may appear every mile or every 5 miles...

The Range Mark Generator is formed by an oscillator and a counter. The frequency of the oscillator is controlled by the Range Adjust Potentiometer (R10). The counter is reset by the main timer and provides equally spaced output pulses. The pulses, or range marks are applied to the Video Amplifier to be mixed with the rest of the RADAR video.
The Echo Position produces a video pulse that will represent the video returned by a target.
The function of the Video Amplifier is to amplify RADAR video from the receiver, range marks from the Range Mark Generator, and any other video signals that a particular system may require.
U3D inverts the pulse and changes it to a square wave. While R12 is used to simulate the Echo Amplifier.
Diode D3 and capacitor C10 mix the two videos together for application to the display. The resulting A Scan representation is applied to the oscilloscope for viewing.
